umc-001: The vulva is the external genitalia: mons pubis, labia, clitoris and vestibule. The vagina is the internal muscular canal running from the vulva to the cervix.
umc-002: The mons pubis is a pad of fatty tissue lying over the symphysis pubis, cushioning it during intercourse. Lubrication comes mainly from Bartholin's glands and the vaginal walls.
umc-003: The clitoris is part of the vulva, the external genitalia. The ovaries, fallopian tubes, uterus (including the cervix) and vagina are the internal organs.
umc-004: An oocyte is an immature egg. It only becomes a mature ovum once meiosis is complete. 'Ova' is simply the plural of ovum, and 'gamete' means any sex cell, male or female.
umc-005: Each pronucleus is haploid (23 chromosomes). When they fuse, the new cell has 46 chromosomes, so it is diploid. It is called a zygote until it starts dividing; 'embryo' comes later.
umc-006: Sperm and eggs are gametes, made by meiosis, so they are haploid: 22 autosomes plus one sex chromosome (X or Y in sperm). Body cells have 46.
umc-007: The fimbriae are finger-like projections at the open end of the fallopian tube. They sweep the released ovum into the tube, which carries it towards the uterus.
umc-008: Follicle growth is driven by FSH. Rising oestrogen from the dominant follicle triggers the LH surge, and it is LH that makes the oocyte complete its first meiotic division and be released. Oestrogen does not mature the oocyte itself.
umc-009: Rising oestrogen triggers a surge of LH from the anterior pituitary, and ovulation follows roughly 24 to 36 hours later.
umc-010: The hypothalamus releases GnRH, which stimulates the anterior pituitary to release FSH and LH. The posterior pituitary releases oxytocin and ADH.
umc-011: After ovulation, the corpus luteum secretes progesterone (and some oestrogen), turning the endometrium secretory and ready for implantation. hCG is made later, by the trophoblast after implantation, and keeps the corpus luteum going.
umc-012: Red blood cells are made in red bone marrow (erythropoiesis). The cardiovascular system transports them, along with nutrients, oxygen, hormones, waste and heat.
umc-013: Perfusion is blood flowing through the capillaries of a tissue. Dilation is a vessel widening; dispersion isn't a cardiovascular term.
umc-014: The superior vena cava returns deoxygenated blood from the head, neck and arms to the right atrium.
umc-015: The right atrium receives deoxygenated blood from the body through the venae cavae. Oxygenated blood from the lungs enters the left atrium through the pulmonary veins.
umc-016: The direction is reversed. The aorta carries oxygenated blood away from the heart (from the left ventricle) to the body.
umc-017: Circulating blood volume rises by about 30 to 50% in pregnancy, roughly 1.5 litres. Plasma rises more than red cell mass.
umc-018: Hypertrophy is an increase in the size of cells, here the heart muscle, as it adapts to the extra volume and workload. Atrophy is wasting.
umc-019: The heart enlarges to cope with the higher blood volume and cardiac output. Oestrogen is credited with stimulating growth of the heart muscle.
umc-020: Plasma volume rises more than red cell mass, so the blood is diluted and haemoglobin concentration falls ('physiological anaemia'). Haemophilia is an inherited clotting disorder; haemochromatosis is iron overload.
umc-021: Respiration also removes carbon dioxide, and includes internal (cellular) respiration, where cells use oxygen to release energy.
umc-022: Tidal volume increases in pregnancy, by about 30 to 40%, as progesterone drives deeper breathing. Room is made by the ribcage widening and the diaphragm rising, not by smaller breaths.
umc-023: The metopic (frontal) suture lies between the two frontal bones. Sagittal: between the parietal bones. Coronal: between the frontal and parietal bones. Lambdoidal: between the parietal and occipital bones.
umc-024: The sagittal suture runs between the two parietal bones, from the anterior to the posterior fontanelle.
umc-025: In a well-flexed cephalic (vertex) presentation the denominator is the occiput. In a face presentation it is the mentum; in a brow presentation, the sinciput (frontal bone).
umc-026: The lambdoidal suture separates the parietal bones from the occipital bone, meeting the sagittal suture at the posterior fontanelle.
umc-027: The bregma is the anterior fontanelle: diamond-shaped, where the frontal, coronal and sagittal sutures meet. The posterior fontanelle is the lambda, which is triangular.
umc-028: When the head is well flexed, the suboccipitobregmatic diameter (9.5 cm) presents, the smallest possible. Submentobregmatic (9.5 cm) presents in a face presentation; suboccipitofrontal (10 cm) when the head is less well flexed.
umc-029: The biparietal diameter, between the parietal eminences, is 9.5 cm. 8.2 cm is the bitemporal diameter.
umc-030: A cephalhaematoma is bleeding under the periosteum, so it can't cross suture lines and appears hours after birth. Caput succedaneum is scalp swelling above the periosteum: it crosses sutures and is present at birth.
umc-031: The sacrococcygeal joint lets the coccyx bend backwards during birth, enlarging the anteroposterior diameter of the outlet.
umc-032: The brim (inlet) is the entrance to the true pelvis; the fetus then passes through the cavity and out of the outlet. 'Inlet' and 'brim' are the same thing, so the second option makes no sense.
umc-033: The pelvic outlet is diamond (lozenge) shaped, not circular. The curve of Carus is the curved path the fetus follows through the cavity and outlet.
umc-034: The gynaecoid pelvis is the most common in women, about half. Its rounded brim is the most favourable shape for birth.
umc-035: Relaxin and progesterone soften the pelvic ligaments and joints; oestrogen increases blood supply and softening of the tissues. Adrenaline and endorphins don't affect the ligaments.
umc-036: Resistance from the pelvic floor increases flexion and makes the head rotate. The pelvic floor's forward slope then guides it round the curve of Carus, so it can extend (deflex) under the pubic arch.
umc-037: The pelvic cavity measures about 12 cm in every diameter. The inlet is widest transversely (13 cm), and the outlet is widest anteroposteriorly (13 cm).
umc-038: Pain is subjective: it is whatever the person says it is. It is shaped by emotion, culture, expectations and previous experience, not just a nervous system reaction.
umc-039: C fibres are unmyelinated, so they conduct slowly and cause a dull, aching, poorly localised pain; they respond mainly to chemical, thermal and mechanical damage. A-delta fibres are myelinated and fast, causing sharp, localised pain.
umc-040: Nociceptors are free nerve endings that detect tissue damage. Chemoreceptors detect chemicals, thermoreceptors temperature, and mechanoreceptors pressure and stretch.
umc-041: Non-painful touch, pressure and warmth stimulate large nerve fibres, which activate inhibitory interneurons in the spinal cord and 'close the gate' on pain signals. This is why massage, warm water and TENS can help in labour.
umc-042: Endorphins are the body's own opioids and rise through labour; oxytocin also has pain-relieving effects. Adrenaline and cortisol are stress hormones. The key also includes prolactin, which rises in labour, but textbooks are less clear on its role in pain relief, so check your lecture notes.
umc-043: In the latent phase the cervix changes (softens, effaces and dilates) up to 4 cm, with painful contractions. Established labour starts from 4 cm with regular painful contractions (NICE).
umc-044: Homeostasis is the body keeping its internal environment (temperature, fluid, pH, blood glucose) stable despite outside changes.
umc-045: Contractions press the presenting part onto the cervix, which triggers more oxytocin and stronger contractions (the Ferguson reflex). This loop amplifies itself until birth. Negative feedback works the opposite way, bringing a value back to its set point.
umc-046: Adrenaline and other catecholamines, released with fear or stress, inhibit oxytocin, so contractions weaken and labour can slow. This is why a calm, private environment matters.
umc-047: A full bladder can block the descent of the presenting part, reduce how well the uterus contracts, and risk bladder trauma. Women are encouraged to empty their bladder regularly in labour.
umc-048: The head descends and flexes, then rotates internally so the occiput comes to the front. It crowns and is born by extension, then restitutes, untwisting to realign with the shoulders. The shoulders rotate internally into the anteroposterior diameter of the outlet, which you see as the head turning externally. The body is born by lateral flexion.
umc-049: After the placenta separates, the interlacing muscle fibres of the myometrium contract and retract, squeezing shut the blood vessels running between them. Together with clotting, this controls bleeding at the placental site.
umc-050: A succenturiate placenta has an accessory lobe joined to the main placenta by vessels running through the membranes. If the lobe is retained, it can cause haemorrhage. Circumvallate: the membranes fold back, leaving a ring on the fetal surface. Bipartite: two roughly equal lobes.
umc-051: In a velamentous insertion, the cord inserts into the membranes and its vessels run unprotected to the placenta. Battledore: the cord inserts at the placenta's edge. Vasa praevia: unprotected vessels lie across the cervix, which can happen with a velamentous insertion.
umc-052: After birth the fundus is at about the level of the umbilicus. It descends roughly 1 cm a day, so by about a week it is halfway between the umbilicus and the symphysis pubis. It usually can't be felt abdominally after about 10 to 14 days.
umc-053: During involution, autolysis is the self-digestion of excess muscle protein by the cells' own enzymes. Ischaemia (reduced blood supply as the uterus contracts) and phagocytosis (clearing debris) are separate parts of the process.
umc-054: The key gives progesterone: pregnancy's high progesterone relaxes the vaginal walls, and as it falls after birth they regain tone and the rugae return, around three weeks after birth. Some textbooks link the rugae returning to oestrogen recovering instead, so check your lecture notes.
umc-055: In the proliferation phase, fibroblasts and new blood vessels form granulation tissue, which looks pink or red. Haemostasis is clotting, inflammation brings redness and swelling, and remodelling strengthens the scar over months.
umc-056: The frontal lobe handles reasoning, planning, problem-solving, personality and emotional expression, as well as voluntary movement.
umc-057: The temporal lobe processes hearing and smell, and is involved in memory and understanding language. The occipital lobe handles vision and the parietal lobe touch and spatial awareness. The cerebellum isn't a lobe; it coordinates movement and balance.
umc-058: The medulla oblongata, in the brainstem, contains the cardiac, vasomotor and respiratory centres, plus reflexes such as swallowing and vomiting. The pons helps regulate breathing; the cerebellum coordinates movement.
umc-059: Afferent (sensory) nerves carry information from the body to the brain and spinal cord. Efferent (motor) nerves carry it from the central nervous system to the body. Afferent arrives, efferent exits.
umc-060: The autonomic system controls involuntary processes such as heart rate, digestion and sweating. The somatic system controls voluntary movement of skeletal muscles.
umc-061: The sympathetic nervous system drives the 'fight or flight' response. The parasympathetic system is 'rest and digest'.
umc-062: Sodium rushes into the nerve cell (depolarisation), then potassium flows out (repolarisation). The sodium-potassium pump then restores the resting state.
umc-063: Storing minerals (calcium and phosphate) and making blood cells are metabolic functions. Mechanical functions are support and movement; protective functions include the skull and ribcage shielding organs.
umc-064: Erythropoiesis, the making of red blood cells, happens in red bone marrow.
umc-065: The alimentary canal is the continuous tube from mouth to anus: mouth, pharynx, oesophagus, stomach, and small and large intestine. Accessory organs such as the liver and pancreas aren't part of it.
umc-066: Enzymes break food down chemically: lipase acts on fats, amylase on starch and trypsin on proteins. Mechanical breakdown is chewing and churning; propulsion is moving food along.
umc-067: Propulsion moves food through the tract. It starts with swallowing (voluntary), followed by peristalsis (involuntary). Chewing is mechanical digestion.
umc-068: Peristalsis is involuntary: waves of smooth muscle contraction controlled by the autonomic and enteric nervous systems.
umc-069: Ptyalism is excessive saliva. Gingivitis (gum inflammation) and epistaxis (nosebleeds) are also common in pregnancy, but they aren't about saliva.
umc-070: Progesterone relaxes smooth muscle, slowing the gut. Food stays longer in the colon, more water is absorbed and constipation follows. It also relaxes the cardiac sphincter, causing heartburn.
umc-071: Placental hormones increase resistance to insulin, leaving more glucose available for the fetus. If the pancreas can't make enough extra insulin, blood sugar rises: gestational diabetes.
umc-072: Gastrulation, in week 3, turns the two-layered embryonic disc into three germ layers. The name comes from the Greek for 'stomach', as it lays down the primitive gut, which is why 'formation of the gut' is the intended answer. The internal organs develop later from the germ layers.
umc-073: The three germ layers are ectoderm, mesoderm and endoderm. Endoderm forms the lining of the gut and airways, the liver and the pancreas. Ectoderm forms skin and the nervous system; mesoderm forms muscle, bone, the heart, blood and kidneys.
umc-074: The neural tube becomes the brain and spinal cord, the central nervous system. Most of the peripheral nervous system comes from neural crest cells. Failure of the tube to close causes neural tube defects such as spina bifida, which folic acid helps prevent.
umc-075: The heart tube starts beating around day 22 after fertilisation, during the fourth week of development. Counted from the last menstrual period, that is about 5 to 6 weeks of gestation, so the key is using embryonic age.
umc-076: Blood flow to the kidneys rises by around half or more in pregnancy, and the glomerular filtration rate by about 50%. Waste is cleared faster, so urea and creatinine levels in the blood are lower than outside pregnancy.
umc-077: Dilated ureters and incomplete bladder emptying leave urine sitting still, where bacteria can multiply. UTIs in pregnancy can spread to the kidneys (pyelonephritis) and are linked to preterm labour.
umc-078: The medulla contains the loops of Henle and collecting ducts, which concentrate urine by reabsorbing water and salts. Urine collects in the renal pelvis and is stored in the bladder; the outer capsule protects the kidney.
umc-079: Plasma makes up about 55% of blood. Red cells make up about 45% (the haematocrit); white cells and platelets less than 1%.
umc-080: O negative red cells carry no A, B or RhD antigens, so a recipient's antibodies won't attack them. That makes O negative the universal red cell donor in emergencies.
umc-081: If a RhD-negative mother has a RhD-positive baby, fetal blood entering her circulation can make her produce anti-D antibodies. These could attack a future RhD-positive baby (haemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn). Anti-D immunoglobulin, given within 72 hours of birth when the baby is RhD positive, prevents this.
umc-082: The fluid in the lymphatic system is called lymph: tissue fluid that has drained into the lymph vessels.
umc-083: The thymus is where T lymphocytes ('T' for thymus) mature and learn not to attack the body's own cells. Strictly, they start in the bone marrow and mature in the thymus. It has nothing to do with the thyroid.
umc-084: Pathogen is the umbrella term for anything that causes disease. Bacteria, viruses, fungi and parasites are all types of pathogen.
umc-085: Diastasis recti is separation of the two rectus abdominis muscles along the midline (linea alba) as the growing uterus stretches the abdominal wall. Symphysis pubis dysfunction is pain from the pelvic joint.
umc-086: Lactogenesis is the breast developing the ability to secrete milk. Stage I begins in mid-pregnancy (colostrum); stage II, copious secretion, follows 2 to 3 days after birth as progesterone falls once the placenta is delivered. Ongoing milk production has its own name, galactopoiesis.
umc-087: Oxytocin causes the milk ejection (let-down) reflex by making the cells around the alveoli contract. Prolactin stimulates milk production.
umc-088: Milk is made by secretory cells lining the alveoli. It flows through the lactiferous ducts to the nipple. Montgomery tubercles are glands on the areola that secrete a protective, lubricating oil.
umc-089: Epigenetics is about how genes are switched on or off without changing the DNA sequence itself. Environmental factors such as diet, stress and smoking can cause these changes, including in the womb.
umc-090: Mastication is chewing: the mechanical breakdown of food in the mouth, mixing it with saliva. Swallowing is called deglutition.
umc2-001: The follicular phase is when follicles grow under FSH and make oestrogen, ending at ovulation. In the luteal phase the corpus luteum makes progesterone. Menstruation and the proliferative and secretory phases belong to the uterine cycle.
umc2-002: After ovulation the empty follicle fills with luteinised cells and becomes the corpus luteum ("yellow body"), which secretes progesterone and some oestrogen.
umc2-003: The uterine (endometrial) cycle is menstruation (shedding), the proliferative phase (the lining rebuilds under oestrogen) and the secretory phase (glands secrete under progesterone, ready for implantation). Follicular and luteal are ovarian phases.
umc2-004: After fertilisation, hCG from the trophoblast keeps the corpus luteum going. It keeps secreting progesterone to maintain the endometrium until the placenta takes over at around 10–12 weeks.
umc2-005: Haploid cells have one set of 23 chromosomes: sperm and egg cells. The zygote is diploid (46), the trophoblast is made of diploid cells, and the zona pellucida is a protein coat, not a cell.
umc2-006: The menstrual cycle runs on the hypothalamus, pituitary and ovaries acting on the uterus. The thymus is where T cells mature.
umc2-007: The uterine wall has three layers: perimetrium (outer covering), myometrium (muscle) and endometrium (lining). "Exometrium" isn't a real term.
umc2-008: The labia minora split at the front to form the hood and frenulum of the clitoris, and join at the back to form the fourchette.
umc2-009: In a hormonal cascade one hormone triggers the release of the next, e.g. GnRH → FSH and LH → oestrogen and progesterone. Homeostasis is the overall balance these systems keep.
umc2-010: The endocrine and nervous systems work together, linked mainly through the hypothalamus and pituitary. Nerves act fast and briefly; hormones act more slowly and for longer.
umc2-011: Hormones are secreted into the blood by endocrine glands, and by some specialised cells, e.g. in the placenta and gut.
umc2-012: Water-soluble hormones such as oxytocin and insulin bind receptors on the cell surface. Fat-soluble ones such as oestrogen and thyroid hormones cross the membrane and bind receptors inside the cell.
umc2-013: The thyroid sits at the front of the neck, below the larynx, wrapped around the trachea. The adrenal glands are the ones above the kidneys.
umc2-014: The pineal gland is a small gland deep in the brain. It secretes melatonin, which helps regulate sleep and daily rhythms.
umc2-015: Epinephrine and adrenaline are the same hormone, secreted by the adrenal medulla. Both names mean "on the kidney", one from Greek and one from Latin.
umc2-016: Vasopressin is antidiuretic hormone (ADH), released by the posterior pituitary. It makes the kidneys hold on to water and narrows blood vessels.
umc2-017: Prolactin makes milk, oxytocin ejects it, and the feedback inhibitor of lactation (FIL) slows production when milk stays in the breast. LH triggers ovulation and has no role in breastfeeding.
umc2-018: GnRH from the hypothalamus triggers FSH and LH release from the anterior pituitary, which drive the ovarian cycle. Insulin, TSH and prolactin aren't part of the cycle.
umc2-019: Rising oestrogen from the dominant follicle triggers an LH surge, and ovulation follows about 24–36 hours later.
umc2-020: Oxytocin is nicknamed the "love hormone" because of its links with bonding, touch and attachment. It also drives contractions and milk ejection.
umc2-021: Prolactin, from the anterior pituitary, stimulates the breast's alveolar cells to make milk. Oxytocin causes the milk ejection reflex and contractions.
umc2-022: Progesterone relaxes smooth muscle throughout the body: airways, blood vessels, gut, ureters and uterus. Relaxin mainly softens ligaments and connective tissue.
umc2-023: The pulmonary arteries carry deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle to the lungs. They're the only arteries that carry deoxygenated blood; the pulmonary veins bring oxygenated blood back to the left atrium.
umc2-024: Veins have wide lumens and thin, stretchy walls, so they hold most of the blood (about 60–70%) at any time.
umc2-025: The mitral (bicuspid) valve lies between the left atrium and left ventricle. The tricuspid valve is on the right; the aortic valve is the exit from the left ventricle.
umc2-026: Stroke volume is the blood pumped by the left ventricle in one beat, about 70 ml at rest. The volume per minute is cardiac output: stroke volume × heart rate.
umc2-027: Heart rate rises by about 10–20 beats per minute in pregnancy. Blood volume, cardiac output and heart muscle mass all increase too.
umc2-028: Thinner blood flows more easily through small vessels, which improves perfusion of the placenta and so the supply to the fetus.
umc2-029: Blood volume rises by about 30–50% in pregnancy (the range in the course key), building a reserve against blood loss at birth. Haemodilution is a result of that rise, not a protection in itself.
umc2-030: Clotting factors, especially fibrinogen, rise and natural anticoagulants fall in pregnancy, to limit bleeding at birth. That's why the risk of venous thromboembolism is higher in pregnancy and the puerperium.
umc2-031: Heart rate rises by about 10–20 beats per minute in pregnancy, which helps raise cardiac output.
umc2-032: A pulse is the pressure wave of each heartbeat travelling along an artery. You feel it where an artery runs near the surface over something firm, such as the radial artery at the wrist.
umc2-033: Blood pressure is written systolic over diastolic, e.g. 120/80. The other three statements are correct.
umc2-034: The key gives heart rate, but heart rate does affect blood pressure: blood pressure depends on cardiac output (heart rate × stroke volume) and how much the vessels resist flow. Position, pregnancy and hormones all affect it too. Check your lecture notes for what this question intends.
umc2-035: Blood pressure is the force blood exerts on the walls of the vessels, usually measured in the arteries in mmHg.
umc2-036: The intercostal muscles between the ribs, with the diaphragm, are the main muscles of breathing. The myometrium is the muscle of the uterus; vastus lateralis and brachialis are limb muscles.
umc2-037: The upper airway is the nose, sinuses, pharynx and larynx. The lower airway starts at the trachea and includes the bronchi.
umc2-038: When you breathe in, the diaphragm contracts and flattens downwards, enlarging the chest so air flows in. It rises again when you breathe out.
umc2-039: The trachea is the widest airway. It divides into bronchi, then bronchioles, ending in tiny alveoli.
umc2-040: Progesterone makes the breathing centre more sensitive to carbon dioxide, so tidal volume rises by about 30–40%, and minute ventilation by a similar amount. The breathing rate hardly changes.
umc2-041: The growing uterus pushes the diaphragm up by about 4 cm, the lower ribs flare, and the volume of air left in the lungs at rest falls. The diaphragm doesn't thicken. Increased blood flow to the lungs does happen but is a circulatory change, so the key's answer is the one that doesn't happen at all.
umc2-042: Oxygen use rises by about 20% in pregnancy, for the fetus and placenta and for the mother's own extra work (heart, breathing, kidneys).
umc2-043: Apnoea means no breathing ("a-" without, "-pnoea" breathing). Slow breathing is bradypnoea; shallow breathing is hypopnoea.
umc2-044: Most pregnant women feel breathless at some point, from hormonal and mechanical changes, so it doesn't necessarily mean disease. Sudden, severe or worsening breathlessness still needs assessing.
umc2-045: Progesterone relaxes smooth muscle, so the airways relax and widen, lowering airway resistance.
umc2-046: The ischial spines are the landmark for station: the presenting part's level is given in centimetres above (−) or below (+) the spines.
umc2-047: The sacrum, five fused vertebrae, is the wedge-shaped bone forming the back of the pelvis. The coccyx is the small tailbone below it.
umc2-048: The symphysis pubis is the joint where the two pubic bones meet at the front, joined by a pad of fibrocartilage. It softens and widens slightly in pregnancy.
umc2-049: The four pelvis shapes are gynaecoid, android, anthropoid and platypelloid. "Hymenoid" isn't one.
umc2-050: The gynaecoid pelvis, with a round brim and roomy cavity, is the most common female shape (about half of women) and the best suited to birth.
umc2-051: At the brim the gynaecoid pelvis measures about 11 cm front to back, 12 cm obliquely and 13 cm side to side, its widest diameter.
umc2-052: At the outlet it's about 13 cm front to back, 12 cm obliquely and 11 cm side to side. The widest diameter turns from side to side at the brim to front to back at the outlet, which is why the baby's head rotates.
umc2-053: The curve of Carus is the curved axis of the birth canal: the baby travels down and back, then curves forwards under the symphysis pubis.
umc2-054: Caput succedaneum is swelling of the scalp from pressure against the cervix in labour. It can cross suture lines and goes within a few days. Blood under the periosteum is a cephalhaematoma, which doesn't cross sutures.
umc2-055: The external auditory meatus is the opening of the ear canal. The tragus is the small flap in front of it; the helix is the outer rim of the ear.
umc2-056: A cleft lip can often be seen on the anomaly scan, but a cleft palate on its own is usually hidden and rarely diagnosed in pregnancy. That's why the newborn examination (NIPE) includes looking at and feeling the palate.
umc2-057: Once the cord is clamped its blood supply stops, and the stump dries out and dies off (dry gangrene), usually separating within 5–15 days.
umc2-058: Edwards' syndrome is trisomy 18. Down's syndrome is trisomy 21 and Patau's syndrome is trisomy 13.
umc2-059: Polydactyly means extra fingers or toes. Fused digits are syndactyly.
umc2-060: Vernix is a white, greasy coating that protects the skin in the womb. There's less of it by term, and current advice is to leave it to absorb, not to wash it off.
umc2-061: Milia are tiny white spots on the nose and face from blocked oil glands. They clear on their own, and parents shouldn't squeeze or pick them. Cradle cap is a different condition.
umc2-062: The ductus arteriosus connects the pulmonary artery to the aorta, so most blood bypasses the fluid-filled lungs. It closes in the days after birth. The foramen ovale connects the two atria.
umc2-063: The ductus venosus carries oxygenated blood from the umbilical vein past the liver into the inferior vena cava. It closes over the days after birth, not within minutes.
umc2-064: Apgar scores are taken at 1 and 5 minutes after birth for every baby, and at 10 minutes if needed.
umc2-065: Red cells are made first in the yolk sac, then mainly in the liver from about 6 weeks. The bone marrow starts making them towards the end of the first trimester and takes over as the main site in the third trimester.
umc2-066: Cystic fibrosis is inherited but isn't a metabolic disorder: it affects mucus and sweat glands. Phenylketonuria, maple syrup urine disease and MCADD are inherited metabolic disorders.
umc2-067: Ossification turns the membranous sutures and fontanelles into bone. The posterior fontanelle closes at about 6–8 weeks and the anterior at about 18 months.
umc2-068: Milk is made by the secretory cells lining the breast's alveoli (also called acini), often called lactocytes. The key's "acini cells" means these alveolar cells.
umc2-069: The lactiferous (milk) ducts carry milk from the alveoli to the openings on the nipple. Montgomery's tubercles are small glands on the areola.
umc2-070: Sucking sends nerve signals to the hypothalamus, and the posterior pituitary releases oxytocin, which squeezes milk out (the let-down).
umc2-071: The same signals make the anterior pituitary release prolactin, which drives milk production for later feeds.
umc2-072: Oxytocin causes the let-down (milk ejection) reflex by contracting the cells around the alveoli. Prolactin makes the milk, and stress hormones such as adrenaline and cortisol can block the let-down.
umc2-073: Casein and whey (the key spells it "caesin") are the two main milk proteins in both breastmilk and formula. Lactoferrin is found mainly in breastmilk.
umc2-074: Breast size depends on fat, genetics and puberty, not on the glandular tissue that makes milk. Small breasts can make plenty of milk.
umc2-075: Ultrasound studies show milk flows as the tongue moves down: the vacuum is strongest when the tongue is at its lowest point.
umc2-076: Biological nurturing is laid-back breastfeeding: the mother reclines and the baby lies on her, which triggers the baby's feeding reflexes and gives skin-to-skin contact. It doesn't change inverted nipples.
umc2-077: In breastmilk, "transfer factors" are components such as lactoferrin that help the baby absorb nutrients like iron. The term is also used for immune molecules, which makes the immune option tempting, but the key's answer is absorption.
umc2-078: Blood is a connective tissue: cells (red cells, white cells and platelets) suspended in plasma.
umc2-079: Platelets gather at a damaged vessel to form a plug and help the clotting process. White cells do phagocytosis; red cells carry oxygen.
umc2-080: Erythrocytes (red blood cells) are the cellular, living part of blood. Hormones, electrolytes and antibodies are molecules dissolved in plasma.
umc2-081: Plasma volume rises by more (about 50%) than red cell mass (about 20–30%), so haemoglobin concentration falls. This is the physiological anaemia of pregnancy.
umc2-082: Sickle cell disease affects the haemoglobin in red blood cells, which become sickle-shaped, stiff and short-lived, and can block small vessels.
umc2-083: Type A blood has A antigens on the red cells and anti-B antibodies in the plasma. Josie can't receive type AB, which carries B antigens, and her children's group depends on both parents.
umc2-084: If an RhD-negative mother carries an RhD-positive baby, fetal cells entering her blood can make her produce anti-D antibodies. These can attack the red cells of a later RhD-positive baby, which is why anti-D injections are offered.
umc2-085: Clotting factors rise in pregnancy to limit bleeding at birth. Together with slower blood flow in the veins and vessel damage at birth, that raises the risk of thromboembolism.
umc2-086: The mesoderm (middle layer) forms muscle, bone, the heart, blood vessels and the kidneys. The ectoderm forms the skin and nervous system; the endoderm forms the lining of the gut and lungs.
umc2-087: Strictly, the solid ball of cells formed by the dividing zygote is the morula (around day 3–4). It becomes a hollow blastocyst by about day 5. Morula isn't offered, so blastocyst is the best answer.
umc2-088: Strictly, neurulation is the formation of the neural tube, which becomes the brain and spinal cord. The notochord forms just before it and triggers it. The notochord is the closest option, but check your lecture notes for how your course defines it.
umc2-089: The embryonic period ends about 8 weeks after fertilisation, and the fetal period follows. Counted from the last period (gestational age), that's about 10 weeks, so check which count a question uses.
umc2-090: By about 31 weeks the organs are formed, so the focus is growth and laying down fat. Most fetal weight gain happens in the third trimester.
umc2-091: Mitosis splits one cell into two identical daughter cells with the full (diploid) set of chromosomes, for growth and repair. Meiosis makes four different haploid cells: eggs or sperm.
umc2-092: The spiral arteries of the uterus are widened by the trophoblast so they pour maternal blood into the spaces around the villi, where gases and nutrients cross. (The usual spelling is syncytiotrophoblast.)
umc2-093: A zygote is diploid: 23 chromosomes from the egg plus 23 from the sperm make 46.
umc2-094: The nervous and endocrine systems keep the body in balance together, linked mainly through the hypothalamus.
umc2-095: The autonomic system runs automatic functions: heartbeat, digestion and the stress response. Pain from the skin, muscles and joints is carried by the sensory nerves of the somatic system.
umc2-096: The central nervous system is the brain and spinal cord, including their grey and white matter. Peripheral nerves make up the peripheral nervous system.
umc2-097: The nucleus is in the cell body. Dendrites receive signals, the axon carries them away, and the nodes of Ranvier are gaps in the axon's myelin coating.
umc2-098: The sympathetic system drives "fight or flight": a faster heart, higher blood pressure and wider airways. The parasympathetic system is "rest and digest".
umc2-099: Visceral pain comes from internal organs, such as the uterus in labour. It's often dull, hard to pinpoint and can be felt elsewhere (referred pain). Injury to bones, ligaments and skin causes somatic pain; damage to a nerve itself causes neuropathic pain.
umc2-100: Beta-endorphin is the body's own opioid. It rises through labour and provides natural pain relief. Glutamate is a neurotransmitter that carries pain signals.
umc2-101: Thermoception is sensing temperature. Proprioception is sensing position and movement; nociception is sensing pain.
umc2-102: Nociceptors are free nerve endings that respond to harmful (noxious) stimuli, such as extreme heat, pressure, or chemicals released by damaged tissue.
umc2-103: In the first days after birth the body gets rid of the extra fluid of pregnancy, so passing a lot of urine (diuresis) is normal. Urine retention isn't normal and needs assessing.
umc2-104: Haemorrhoids are common after birth, from pressure in pregnancy, pushing and constipation. A wound breaking open (dehiscence) is a complication, not a normal finding.
umc2-105: Clotting factors stay raised for several weeks after birth, so the risk of thromboembolism continues through the puerperium and is highest in the first weeks.
umc2-106: Diastasis recti is the separation of the two vertical abdominal muscles (rectus abdominis) along the midline. It's common after pregnancy.
umc2-107: Soon after birth the uterus is at or just below the umbilicus. It shrinks by about 1 cm a day and usually can't be felt through the abdomen by 10–14 days.
umc2-108: Wound healing goes haemostasis (clotting), then inflammation, then proliferation (new tissue), then remodelling.
umc2-109: Lochia goes from rubra (red, the first few days) to serosa (pink-brown, from about day 4) to alba (yellow-white, up to about 6 weeks). "Marrona" isn't a real term.
umc2-110: The puerperium lasts about 6 weeks (42 days) after birth, while the body returns to its non-pregnant state.
umc2-111: Relaxin comes mainly from the corpus luteum and placenta, so its level falls once the placenta is delivered. Ligaments regain their tone over the following months.
umc2-112: Suckling releases oxytocin, which contracts the uterus as well as ejecting milk, so breastfeeding helps involution. That's why women may feel afterpains while feeding.
umc2-113: The musculoskeletal system is bones, muscles, cartilage, ligaments, tendons and bursae. The sclera is the white of the eye.
umc2-114: New blood cells are made in the red bone marrow, inside flat bones and the ends of long bones.
umc2-115: The heart is made of cardiac muscle, a type of its own. Smooth muscle lines the bronchi, uterus, gut and blood vessels.
umc2-116: The pelvis has cartilaginous joints: the symphysis pubis and the joint between the sacrum and coccyx. The skull's sutures are fibrous joints, and most limb joints are synovial.
umc2-117: Hypertrophy is growth in the size of cells, as in heart muscle in pregnancy. Hyperemesis gravidarum is severe vomiting in pregnancy.
umc2-118: Tendons are cords of tough connective tissue linking muscle to bone. Ligaments link bone to bone.
umc2-119: Haematopoiesis is the making of all blood cells: red cells, white cells and platelets. Making only red cells is erythropoiesis.
umc2-120: Progesterone relaxes the smooth muscle in vessel walls, so vascular resistance falls in pregnancy, not rises. Slower gut transit, a quiet uterus and lower airway resistance are all progesterone effects.
umc2-121: Relaxin softens the mother's ligaments, loosening the pelvis (which can cause pelvic girdle pain), and plays a part in tissue repair. Moulding is the baby's skull bones overlapping under pressure in labour; relaxin doesn't cause it.
umc2-122: As the uterus grows, the centre of gravity moves forward, the pelvis tilts forward and the lower back curves more (lumbar lordosis).
umc2-123: The kidneys filter waste, balance electrolytes and make erythropoietin. Uterine contractions are driven by oxytocin and prostaglandins.
umc2-124: Blood flow to the kidneys rises by about 50–60% in pregnancy (the range in the course key). Plasma volume rises, the ureters widen and lengthen, and UTIs become more likely.
umc2-125: Proteinuria of 2+ is abnormal in pregnancy and needs following up, as it can be a sign of pre-eclampsia, especially with raised blood pressure. Nitrites (the key says "nitrates") suggest infection, glucose can appear with gestational diabetes, and blood needs investigating.
umc2-126: Leukocytes, nitrites (written "nitrates" in the key) and blood suggest a UTI. Glucose doesn't: in pregnancy it's more often because the kidneys let more glucose through, or a sign of diabetes.
umc2-127: The rise in plasma volume and cardiac output, with relaxed blood vessels, increases blood flow to the kidneys. Progesterone rises in pregnancy; it doesn't fall.
umc2-128: The cortex is the outer layer of the kidney and holds most of the filtering units (glomeruli). The medulla, with its pyramids, is inside, and the calyces collect urine.
umc2-129: Each ureter carries urine from a kidney to the bladder. The urethra drains the bladder, and the nephron is the kidney's functional unit.
umc2-130: The renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system (RAAS) raises blood pressure. When pressure falls, the kidneys release renin, which leads to narrower vessels and salt and water retention.
umc2-131: GFR is the glomerular filtration rate: how much blood the kidneys filter per minute. It rises by about 50% in pregnancy.
umc2-132: Asymptomatic bacteriuria is bacteria in the urine without symptoms. It's screened for in pregnancy because, untreated, it can lead to pyelonephritis (kidney infection).
umc2-133: Antibodies bind to specific pathogens, neutralising them and marking them for destruction. Phagocytes, not antibodies, engulf pathogens.
umc2-134: Passive immunity is receiving ready-made antibodies, through the placenta or breastmilk. Vaccination and infection give active immunity, where the body makes its own antibodies.
umc2-135: Innate immunity responds quickly but in the same way to any threat, and has no memory. Antibodies, specific recognition and memory belong to adaptive immunity.
umc2-136: B cells (which make antibodies) and T cells drive adaptive immunity. Macrophages, neutrophils and natural killer cells are part of innate immunity.
umc2-137: Skin, mucus and stomach acid are physical and chemical barriers. Fever is a whole-body response to infection, not a barrier.
umc2-138: In pregnancy the white cell count rises, some immune responses are damped so the fetus isn't rejected, and susceptibility to some viruses and to thrush (vulval yeast infection) increases. So decreased susceptibility to thrush isn't normal.
umc2-139: At term around 500–750 ml of blood a minute flows to the uterus and placenta. Once the placenta is delivered, the uterus contracts hard and its criss-crossed muscle fibres squeeze the blood vessels shut ("living ligatures"), so blood flow to the uterus falls sharply. Clotting at the placental site helps stop bleeding, but it isn't a change in volume.
